Items.Authors: Maria Grazia Labate, Grazia Umana, Ugo Di Giammatteo, Corrado Trigilio, Pietro Bolli, Andrea Melis, Francesco Schillirò, Francesco Cavallaro, Enrico Giro, Rodolfo Canestrari, Adriano Fontana, Gianfranco Fallica, Tonino Pisanu, Pasqualino Marongiu, Carolina Belli, Kobus Cloete, Sipho Ngunyule, Sibongile Nong, Scarre Celliers, Sias Malan, Ruan de Lange, Renier Siebrits, Wesley Newton, Tyrone van Balla, George Isoe, Ofaletse Mokone, Marc Welz, Hendrik Bester, Ben Jordaan
Items.Title: Enabling high-frequency capability on the MeerKAT radio telescope in the SKA era: The STILES MeerKAT Band 5B project
Items.Abstract: The MeerKAT Band 5B project will extend the telescope’s high-frequency capability by deploying 64 newly developed cryogenic receivers, along with down-convertering digitizers, backend systems, and supporting infrastructure.  Operating in the SKA-Mid Band 5b range (8.3–15.4 GHz), this upgrade will make MeerKAT the most sensitive centimeter-wave interferometer in the southern hemisphere until SKA becomes fully operational. Since MeerKAT currently lacks access to these frequencies and SKAO will not retrofit band 5 onto the MeerKAT antennas, this project uniquely enables capability that would otherwise not be realized, providing Band 5B ahead of time and serving as a technological and scientific precursor.   Designed to meet SKA specifications, Band 5B ensures sustained scientific value into the SKA era.  All procurement activities have been completed. By November 2025, all receivers had been manufactured and almost fully delivered to site, and all 64 digitizer D-Engines manufactured and test

Items.Authors: Raphaël Pourcelot, Laurent Pueyo, Rémi Soummer, Marshall D. Perrin, Emiel H. Por, Sarah Steiger, Randal Telfer
Items.Title: JWST telemetry combined with active coronagraphy: inferring raw contrast predictions for exoplanet imaging with future large space observatory
Items.Abstract: NASA’s Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) aims to detect and study Earth-like exoplanets, which will require maintaining some wavefront error mode at a picometric stability over hours. While the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) achieves sub-nanometer stability, it lacks the advanced coronagraphy and active wavefront control needed for direct imaging of such planets.  To better understand the technology gap to be bridged by HWO, we combine JWST’s segments phasing in-flight data, a modern Apodized Pupil Lyot Coronagraph (APLC) design, and wavefront control techniques from the Roman Space Telescope’s Coronagraph Instrument (CGI) to simulate residual wavefront errors under realistic conditions. We evaluate different system designs, including deformable mirror and sensor configurations, to determine achievable contrast levels. The pairing these simulations with JWST’s stability measurements provides insight of the current technological capabilities for Earth-like planet imaging.

Items.Authors: José L. Ortiz, Jaime Robles, Jorge Avarias, Ricardo Carrasco, Johnny Reveco, Sebastian Rodriguez, Gastón Vélez, Jose Lobos, Baltasar Vila-Vilaro, Javier Rojas, Vicente Aitken, Jason Castro
Items.Title: Managing critical and large-scale obsolescence at ALMA: the E2C deployment project
Items.Abstract: The ALMA Observatory, with 66 radiotelescopes and other central systems, has operated for nearly 15 years and is undergoing major upgrades while needing to maintain aging infrastructure. The Ethernet-To-CAN (E2C) project addressed obsolescence by replacing ALMA’s legacy real-time control computers. This paper focuses on the E2C Deployment Project, covering the manufacturing, installation, testing, and acceptance of the new devices. As ALMA’s first observatory-wide hardware upgrade, the deployment had to be completed during record observing output, tightly aligned with the Cycle 12 software release, and fully compliant with new cybersecurity requirements. Despite these constraints, the project finished on schedule and with minimal operational impact thanks to detailed planning, early risk and failure mitigation, extensive unit and system validation, and disciplined yet adaptable execution.

Items.Authors: Fengchuan Liu
Items.Title: Progress update on the Thirty Meter Telescope (TMT) project
Items.Abstract: TMT is an extremely large optical-infrared telescope (ELT) with diffraction-limited performance, the only ELT in the northern hemisphere. As part of the US ELT program, TMT received the top ranking in Astro2020 and passed the NSF PDR in 2023. A December 2024 report from a NSF external review on US ELT recommended entering TMT to NSF final design phase. The US President's FY2026 Budget Request to Congress, however, left TMT outside of the NSF final design process. This presented a significant challenge in the path forward and to the progress TMT has made in building relationships with communities in Hawaii. Members of TMT International Observatory remain committed in finding a path forward, including evaluating a generous offer from the Government of Spain to build the observation in Spain. This paper will describe the latest technical progress in TMT’s design and development in all partner countries, and the many challenges and opportunities of managing a truly global collaboration.

Items.Authors: Karine Mercier
Items.Title: Two years of operational life for SVOM French Instruments
Items.Abstract: The SVOM (Space-based multi-band astronomical Variable Objects Monitor) French-Chinese mission is dedicated to the detection, localization and study of Gamma Ray Bursts (GRBs) and other high-energy transient phenomena. Two instruments ECLAIRs and MXT are developed under the responsibility of the National French Space Agency (CNES), for GRB detection in Gamma ray band and fine localize and observe the follow-up in soft X-ray band. After a reminder of the instruments’ design, at first, we will provide details on instruments validation on the Chinese satellite, including the main results. In second time, it will presented the results of the commissioning of the instruments in flight and detailing the main corrections made to optimize performances.

Items.Authors: Elijah Kane, Chris Albert, Andrew Beyer, Charles Bradford, Pierre Echternach, Logan Foote, Jason Glenn, Henry LeDuc, Jonas Zmuidzinas
Items.Title: Ultrasensitive kilo-pixel kinetic inductance detector arrays for PRIMA FIRESS: preserving sensitivity in the space radiation environment
Items.Abstract: The Probe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics (PRIMA) is a proposed space observatory at wavelengths between 25 and 265 microns. Kinetic inductance detector (KID) arrays fabricated for PRIMA at the NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory have achieved background-limited sensitivities for the space environment. In this talk, I summarize the yield and sensitivity of prototype arrays for PRIMA’s spectrometer, FIRESS. I also discuss the measures taken to qualify the arrays for use in the energetic proton environment of the L2 orbit. We demonstrate that a backside metal layer is effective in reducing cosmic ray glitch rates and infer a dead time due to proton impacts of well below 10%. We have also performed an experiment to demonstrate that total dose is not a concern for aluminum KIDs. We cryogenically irradiate the array with alpha particles to many times the expected total displacement damage dose in PRIMA’s 5-year lifetime, finding no change in performance.

Items.Authors: Maren Cosens, Nicholas P. Konidaris, Gwen C. Rudie, Andrew B. Newman, Leon Aslan, Robert Barkhouser, Christoph Birk, Julia Brady, Mathias Gumy, Tyson Hare, Stephen C. Hope, Charlie Hull, Daniel D. Kelson, Gerrad Killion, Alicia Lanz, Solange Ramirez, Cyril Rupf, Patricio Schurter, William Schoenell, Stephen A. Smee, Peter Spanoudakis, Jason E. Williams
Items.Title: Update on the Magellan InfraRed Multi-Object Spectrograph (MIRMOS)
Items.Abstract: The Magellan InfraRed Multi-Object Spectrograph (MIRMOS) will be a next generation multi-object (MOS) and integral field spectrograph (IFS) for the 6.5m Magellan telescopes at Las Campanas Observatory in Chile. MIRMOS will perform R~3700 spectroscopy over a simultaneous wavelength range of 0.886 - 2.404um (Y, J, H, and K bands) in addition to imaging over the range of 0.7 - 0.886um. Target selection in the MOS mode is achieved through a cryogenic mechanism capable of making up to 92 slits over a 13’x3’ field of view (FoV). The IFS mode of operation for MIRMOS will be achieved via an image slicer style integral field unit (IFU) which provides an ~18”x26” FoV made up of 0.84”x26” slices. We will describe here the design of the MIRMOS instrument -- now through the preliminary design phase -- and provide an update on the project timeline.

Items.Authors: Matthijs Mars, Sebastiaan Y. Haffert, Joseph D. Long, Rico Landman, Louis Desdoigts, Olivier Guyon, Jared R. Males, Laird M. Close, Kyle van Gorkum, Alexander D. Hedglen, Sandrine Juillard
Items.Title: Physics-informed digital twin for forward modelling low-order aberrations in high-contrast imaging
Items.Abstract: We develop a physics-informed, fully differentiable digital twin of a high-contrast imager’s science path and low-order wavefront sensor to forward-model residual low-order aberrations and reconstruct the stellar PSF. By explicitly modelling the aberrations measured by the LOWFS, the approach improves stellar leakage subtraction compared to methods that rely solely on science camera data. This hybrid physics/data framework improves robustness, reduces calibration requirements, and adapts easily to different coronagraph configurations. We present initial laboratory validation on MagAO-X, demonstrating the feasibility of telemetry-driven forward modelling.

Items.Authors: William J. Marshall, Shannon Fitton, Megan Dubay, Henry Corbett, Nicholas M. Law, Alex Bucheli, Jonathan Carney, James Dockery, Lawrence Machia, Thomas Procter, Michael Ronco, Donovan Schlekat, Alan Vasquez Soto
Items.Title: Electron umbrellas and photon rain: An investigation into several noise and charge effects in CMOS detectors
Items.Abstract: Astronomical surveys like the upcoming Argus Array, a 1,200-telescope optical survey instrument which will image 8,000 square degrees every minute, rely on the combination of many images from CMOS detectors to meet their scientific objectives. It is therefore important to know exactly how the images from these detectors behave when stacked. Here, we show that certain artifacts, which may not cause issues in single frames, could become relevant when large numbers of these images are co-added for additional depth. We have conducted an investigation into the behavior of one such class of artifact, here referred to as “umbrellas” for their shape, and their potential impact on image calibration and co-addition. These artifacts appear 100s of times in every Sony IMX455 and IMX461 image we examined and pollute 10-15 nearby pixels each. We discuss hot pixel detection methods and calibration routines which will mitigate the impact of these artifacts on Argus science products.

Items.Authors: Ettore Pedretti, Alasdair Milne, Robert R. Thomson, Berke Ricketti, Andy Vick
Items.Title: Multi-mode photonic beam combination for long-baseline interferometry
Items.Abstract: Single-mode photonic technologies, such as fiber-based and integrated-optics beam combiners, have revolutionized optical and infrared interferometry by providing spatial filtering that mitigates atmospheric turbulence. This improves calibration of squared visibilities and closure phases but reduces throughput and increases sensitivity to photometric fluctuations. Adaptive optics can boost coupling efficiency but introduces aberrations. We explore a multi-mode photonic beam combiner using photonic lanterns to convert multimode light into multiple single-mode outputs. Simulations evaluate coupling efficiency and throughput under realistic conditions, comparing performance to conventional single-mode designs and outlining implications for next-generation long-baseline interferometric instruments.

Items.Authors: James A. Green, Shari Breen, Sharmila Goedhart, Andre van Es
Items.Title: Ramping up SKAO Science Operations for SKA-Low Science Verification
Items.Abstract: Significant progress is being made with the construction and commissioning of the SKA-Low telescope in Australia at Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, the CSIRO Murchison Radio-astronomy Observatory site. Concurrent with telescope deployment, is the ramp up of telescope operations in order to deliver on the promise of the SKAO to the scientific community. We will discuss the pathway to the SKA-Low telescope surpassing current comparable radio astronomy facilities. With Array Assembly 2, SKAO will conduct its initial Science Verification, providing the community with its first access to SKAO data. The intention of Science Verification is to confirm the end-to-end system functionality of modes and capabilities, in order to build trust within the community, and expose the community to SKA data. We will provide a description of the scaling up of scientific operations with the array assembly deployments, including, scheduling, observing, monitoring and processing of data.

Items.Authors: Anastasia Galkin, Kirill Makan, Simeon Reusch, Wail Abbas Ahmed, Ole Streicher, Jakob Walcher
Items.Title: The 4MOST public archive (4PA)
Items.Abstract: The Research Data Infrastructure (RDI) group at the Leibniz Institute for Astrophysics is leading the development and implementation of the 4PA, the 4MOST Survey Public Archive. The DRI group provides data curation expertise to shape the flow of data from raw data to scientific products useful to the scientific community. Data published in the 4PA will include processed Level 1 data, as well as Level 2 science products derived from Level 1 data. We have successfully established a data release management process and contributed to data models and metadata enrichment to make the future archive more useful. Data releases will first be made available to the 4MOST science community. After the proprietary period agreed upon with ESO, the data will be made publicly available. We have successfully developed the archive's software architecture, which is based on the Daiquiri framework, developed by AIP, and the containerized environment dq-dev.

Items.Authors: Joost A. van den Born, Rico Landman, David S. Doelman, Frans Snik, Yuki Nishie, Yuta Watanabe, Masakazu Shoda, Felix Bettonvil, Ester Aranzana, Jeroen Rietjens, Pierre Baudoz, Olivier Absil, Gilles Orban de Xivry, Dennis Dolkens
Items.Title: Vector apodizing phase plates for the ELT: from prototype to final optics for METIS and MICADO
Items.Abstract: The first generation of instruments for the upcoming Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) will allow for the direct imaging of many exoplanets that were previously below the sensitivity or resolution limits of existing facilities. Three different Vector Apodizing Phase Plates, a liquid crystal based pupil coronagraph, will be available in both first light instruments; two in METIS, the mid-infrared imaging and spectroscopy instrument, and one in MICADO, the near infrared imaging instrument. In this work, we will present an overview of the current status of these optics, including the manufacturing, lab measurements and discuss the expected final performance.

Items.Authors: Mayukh Bagchi, Felix M. Thiel, Laura M. Fissel, Lindy L. Blackburn, Rafael Costa, Vincent L. Fish, Daryl Haggard, Michael D. Johnson, Maggie Oxford, Ganesh Rajagopalan, Javier L. Romualdez, Aarchi Shah, Adrian K. Sinclair, Stephanie St-Jean, Terry Yang
Items.Title: An RFSoC-based backend and timing system for the balloon‑borne very long baseline interferometry experiment
Items.Abstract: We present a novel RFSoC-based digital backend and precision timing system for the Balloon-borne Very Long Baseline Interferometry Experiment (BVEX), a 22 GHz pathfinder mission for future high-frequency stratospheric mobile VLBI stations. The system employs an AMD-Xilinx RFSoC 4x2 for a high-resolution spectrometer and real-time 2-bit requantization of 4.096 GSPS sampled data, streaming at 8.2 Gbps via 100 Gigabit Ethernet to a 16 TB NVMe storage array. Timing stability is maintained by a Rakon OCXO with continuous GPS-based drift monitoring at 60-picosecond resolution. Ground testing validated system performance, demonstrating exceptional timing stability despite platform dynamics. This represents the first deployment of RFSoC-based VLBI instrumentation and precise timing systems on balloon platforms. For the 2027 reflight, we are implementing enhanced thermal management and expanded storage capacity, along with direct NIC to NVMe firmware, for improved power efficiency.

Items.Authors: Shahab O. Dabironezare, Giulia Conenna, Daan Roos, Dimitry Lamers, Daniela Perez Capelo, Hendrik M. Veen, David J. Thoen, Vishal Anvekar, Stephen J. C. Yates, Robert Huiting, Jochem J. A. Baselmans
Items.Title: Experimental demonstration of the optical coupling for an array of lens-absorber coupled KIDs operating at 6.98 THz for PRIMA
Items.Abstract: Focal plane arrays of silicon lenses with distributed absorbers coupled to Kinetic Inductance Detectors (KIDs) are the chosen detector technology for the hyperspectral imager of the PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics (PRIMA). In this contribution we present the modelling approach, design, fabrication, and experimental verification for a 25-pixel lens-absorber KID array operating at the central frequency of 6.98 THz. The aperture efficiency of the detectors is measured to be 54%. We verified this against numerical simulations using an in-house developed efficient spectral technique and find an excellent agreement. The noise equivalent power of the KIDs is also measured with a limiting value of 8×10^(-20)W/√Hz under negligible optical loading. These experimental verifications indicate that the modelling, design, realisation and characterisation of the proposed detectors are well understood, paving the way for the development of the flight chips for PRIMA’s hyperspectral imager.

Items.Authors: Breann N. Sitarski, Theodore J. Hadjimichael, George M. Hilton, Babak N. Saif, David Baran, Michael J. Eisenhower, Sang Park, Marcel Bluth, James M. Whipple, Stephen P. Chaykovsky, Stephen J. Hagopian, Elliot C. Schwartz, Jordan M. Effron, Michael Chapman, Brian S. Abresch, Dawn L. Blackburn, Thomas P. Zielinski, Brooke Turner, Colby D. Moore
Items.Title: Mini-Metrology and Ultra-Stable Testbed (Mini-MUST): a TRL-advancing stability testbed for Habitable Worlds Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) requires unprecedented, picometer-level stability to fulfill one of its driving science requirements of detecting and characterizing Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars. Over the last several years, the Goddard Space Flight Center’s Ultra-Stable Structures Laboratory has been designing and constructing the Mini-Metrology and Ultra-Stable Testbed (Mini-MUST) to test components and systems to these stability levels and advance their technical readiness levels. Mini-MUST recently achieved first light at GSFC and has started testing campaigns to support the ROSES D.19 projects. We present our first light results, including correlation of our measured data with our high-fidelity thermal and structural models.

Items.Authors: Hangxin Ji, Ru Chen, Yong Li, Cheng Liao, Haoran Yu, Jun Li, Qinyang Dong, Lei Wang
Items.Title: Multi-object fiber spectrograph for the 4-m class Jiao Tong University Spectroscopic Telescope (JUST)
Items.Abstract: The JUST telescope is a 4-m class, wide-field segmented facility dedicated to massively multiplexed spectroscopy. We present the optical and system design of its Multi-Object Fiber Spectrograph (MOFS), supporting up to 2,000 fibers across a 1.2° Nasmyth field. The instrument employs a three-channel layout (365–560nm, 540–745nm, 720–925nm) using dichroics, high-efficiency VPH gratings, and fast f/1.4 cameras fed by a 175-mm collimated beam. With optimized fiber-slit geometry, MOFS delivers R≈2,000–5,000 and >60% peak throughput. Each exposure records over 500 spectra and scales to the full survey capacity. One spectrograph also accommodates a compact 19-fiber IFU for spatially resolved studies of transients and compact objects. Engineered for stability at the 4,300-m site and optimized for faint targets, MOFS will enable dense mapping of large-scale structures, time-domain follow-ups, and coordinated surveys with WFST and CSST, advancing JUST as a next-generation spectroscopic facility.

Items.Authors: Andrew W. Serio, Natalia McCarthy, Sandra Ortiz, Randy Gay, Mei Starns, Loreto Troncoso, Hernan Chacana, Angelica Junco
Items.Title: NOIRLab's business operations standardization effort
Items.Abstract: NSF NOIRLab, funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF), was formed in 2019 by consolidating three observatories (NOAO, International Gemini Observatory, and NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory). As a result, NOIRLab inherited disparate operational processes and toolsets leading to increased operational complexity and higher costs, creating inefficiencies that hinder effective, unified operations. We launched a business operations standardization effort with Atlassian(™) tools selected as the supporting software platform. We implemented a standardized Project Management framework for milestones and work packages, a service desk to standardize organizational processes like documentation registration, hiring, and project submission and evaluation, and a centralized database to consolidate operational data. This effort enables effective reporting, performance evaluation, and informed decision-making with data from a single source of truth. This paper details this initiative.

Items.Authors: Robin Swanson, Suresh Sivanandam
Items.Title: Post facto photon fixing
Items.Abstract: Single photon avalanche detectors (SPADs) have emerged as a potential successor of current wavefront sensor (WFS) and science camera detectors. Due to their lack of readout noise and ability to operate at very high frame-rates they are particularly well suited for low flux imaging -- as is often the case when observing with an adaptive optics (AO) system. However, while the underlying detector technologies are radically different, current applications of SPADs in AO settings have treated them simply as standard CMOS sensors with desirable noise properties. In this work we present a new method which takes advantage of the SPADs high-frame rates when used as a science camera. We show how by deconvolving science images using information from their associated residual WFS slopes, we can undo certain effects caused by servo-lag. We show that our method is capable of improving both Strehl ratio and contrast in simulation as well as preliminary experimental results.

Items.Authors: Jean-Gabriel Cuby, Kara Dumaguin, Christine Matsuda, Rich Matsuda, John O'Meara
Items.Title: Astronomy's relationship with the lands and communities of Maunakea: an update
Items.Abstract: In 2023, leaders of Maunakea Observatories shared their perspective on the historic events surrounding the controversy in Hawaiʻi over the development of astronomical facilities on Maunakea. In this paper, we shared our process of introspection and transformation, our hopes and ambitions for the future of astronomy in Hawaiʻi, as advocated by the U.S. National Academy of Sciences and Engineering's Astro2020 report, which calls on the profession to embrace a community-based model of astronomy. We called on the entire profession, including astronomers, engineers, technicians and administrative staff, to share their thoughts and help us develop this model.    In this paper, we will review the progress of this model, particularly in Hawaiʻi, and reflect on the opportunities and initiatives still to be taken to consolidate and expand it.

Items.Authors: Benjamin Fulton, Jennifer Burt, Chad Bender, Andreas Quirrenbach, Andreas Seifahrt, Andrew Howard, Andy Szentgyorgyi, Cem Onyuksel, Chas Beichman, Damien Ségransan, Daniel Holdsworth, Emile Fontanet, Daniel M. Krolikowski, Étienne Artigau, Gaspare Lo Curto, Jonathan Crass, Julian Sturmer, Lars Buchhave, Leonardo Paredes, Lily Zhao, Marshall Johnson, Martino Romaniello, Megan Bedell, Michelle Edwards, Neil Cook, Rose Gibson, Sam Halverson, Sarah Logsdon, Sean Carey, Tanya Das, Xavier Dumusque, Timothy Pickering, Joris De Ridder, Saskia Prins
Items.Title: Developing a community EPRV data standard
Items.Abstract: The latest Extreme Precision Radial Velocity (EPRV) spectrographs have now collected enough data to study how instrument-specific hardware and software choices affect final RVs and stellar variability metrics. Our team has defined an EPRV data standard and 'translator' tools to enable cross-instrument comparisons and reveal previously hidden small-scale systematics. The standard also offers a starting point for new instruments, reducing the burden of developing independent formats and pipelines. We will present the first release, covering products from order-by-order spectra to derived RVs, along with translator templates that support coordinated comparisons of stellar data across EPRV spectrographs.

Items.Authors: Amélie Crebassa-Néron, Hélène T. Krol, Xavier Buet, Pierre-Louis Martin, Didier Torricini, Grégory Chauveau, Joost van den Born, Annemieke Janssen, Ester Aranzana
Items.Title: Narrow-band filters coatings for the cryogenic subsystem of the MICADO instrument
Items.Abstract: MICADO, the first-light near-infrared camera for the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), is designed to deliver unprecedented precision imaging for studies of galaxy evolution, the Galactic Center and its supermassive black hole, as well as the characterization of exoplanets and circumstellar disks. Installed under high vacuum and operated at cryogenic temperatures (~80 K), MICADO covers the 0.8–2.45 μm spectral range using two large filter wheels populated with broadband, intermediate-band, and narrow-band filters.  In the frame of this project, CILAS was in charge of the development of the narrow-band filter coatings. These filters must meet stringent optical and mechanical requirements to ensure high spectral stability and transmission in the cryogenic environment of the instrument.   We describe the design approach, coating technologies, and validation strategy implemented to guarantee performance at operating temperature.

Items.Authors: Frederic Lemmel, Vincent Affatato, Eloy Hernandez, Thibaut Prod'Homme, Malik Mansour
Items.Title: Pyxel 3.0: New features and applications for the collaborative instrument simulator
Items.Abstract: Pyxel is an open-source and collaborative Python-based framework for simulating imaging instruments with a strong focus on detector modelling. Pyxel version 3 introduces major enhancements, including preconfigured simulation pipelines for a catalogue of widely used detectors (e.g. Te2v CIS304, Leonardo IBEX, Teledyne HxRG) accessible through a new GUI, and support for focal-plane and multi-channel detector simulations.   With a rapidly growing community beyond the original ESA-ESO collaboration and contributions from CEA-Saclay, MSSL, CRAL and ISAE-Supaero, Pyxel is now used in numerous projects, including ESA’s Arrakihs mission.

Items.Authors: Mona El Morsy, Elizabeth Arcadi, Simon Gross, Stephanie Rossini-Bryson, Barnaby Norris, Glen Douglass, Peter Tuthill, Olivier Guyon, Julien Lozi, Thayne Currie, Sebastien Vievard, Marc-Antoine Martinod, Nemanja Jovanovic
Items.Title: Starlight suppression with photonic integrated circuits: laboratory characterization and future applications for Subaru/GLINT and HWO
Items.Abstract: Directly imaging Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars requires starlight suppression on the order of ~10⁻¹⁰ . Nulling interferometry offers a pathway to achieve this extreme level of suppression at small angular separations challenging to coronagraphs (~1–2 λ/D), by suppressing stellar light through destructive interference while transmitting off-axis planet light. Photonic integrated circuits (PICs) have emerged as compact, stable platforms for implementing nulling interferometers.  In this talk, we describe the laboratory characterization of one such application of PICs for GLINT on Subaru and HWO, tested at UTSA and developed by Macquarie University. Our design focuses on a photonic chip incorporating an integrated thermal phase shifter. We describe how this approach differs from that of conventional PICs, where the thermal phase shifter in our setup provides an active tuning to correct for optical path differences and thus sustaining deep null performance.

Items.Authors: Kaitlyn Hessel, Christian Marois, Christopher Mann, William Thompson, Sébastien Fabbro, Adam Johnson, Olivier Lardière, Andre Fogal, Joeleff Fitzsimmons
Items.Title: On-sky coherent differential imaging with a self coherent camera: classical and machine learning pipelines
Items.Abstract: Coherent Differential Imaging (CDI) is a direct imaging post-processing technique that suppresses quasi-static speckles to isolate planetary signals. By exploiting the incoherence of planet and star light, CDI reconstructs the speckle field for subtraction, offering theoretically infinite contrast. Limitations in point spread function reconstruction and chromaticity constrain lab gains to ~30x using a Self Coherent Camera (SCC). We present the first on-sky CDI results with an SCC in the Subaru Pathfinder Instrument for Detecting Exoplanets and Retrieving Spectra (SPIDERS). We also investigate a machine learning (ML) approach to CDI to mitigate chromaticity and increasing contrast gains. These results demonstrate CDI’s capabilities on-sky with an SCC using both classical and ML pipelines, paving the way to deployment with the CAL2 system on the Gemini Planet Imager 2 and future development on the Habitable World’s Observatory, enabling detection of closer-in, lower-mass exoplanets.

Items.Authors: Giulia Conenna, Stephen Yates, Kenichi Karatsu, Anaïs Besnard, Valentin Sauvage, Daniela Perez Capelo, Dimitry Lamers, David Thoen, Martijn Veen, Jochem J. A. Baselmans, Lorenza Ferrari
Items.Title: Radiation qualification of lens-absorber and antenna-coupled kinetic inductance detectors for the PRIMA mission
Items.Abstract: Despite significant progress in far-infrared detector technology, demonstrating radiation hardness remains a critical step for space qualification. This is particularly relevant for the PRIMA mission, which require detectors capable of operating reliably over a decade in the L2 environment.  PRIMAger includes two KID designs: single-polarized leaky-lens antenna-coupled KIDs for the Polarimetric Imager (PPI), and lens-absorber-coupled KIDs for the Hyperspectral Imager (PHI). All devices are based on NbTiN resonators with an aluminum section for radiation absorption. PHI uses absorbers on solid Si, whereas PPI uses an aluminum coplanar waveguide coupled to an antenna fabricated on a 100 nm SiN membrane.  During the test campaign conducted at PARTREC (the Netherlands), our prototypes were cooled down in the DRACuLA cryostat to 120 mK and exposed to proton-beam radiation corresponding to the total dose expected over ten years at L2. The results show negligible degradation in key parameters.

Items.Authors: Jeffrey S. Smith, Lee D. Feinberg, John K. Ziemer
Items.Title: Habitable Worlds Observatory: project status
Items.Abstract: The Habitable Worlds Observatory Technology Maturation Project Office (HWO-TMPO) is executing a comprehensive pre-formulation program to mature critical technologies and mission architectures for NASA's next flagship astrophysics mission following Roman. Established in August 2024 in response to the 2020 Decadal Survey's top large mission recommendation, HWO-TMPO has systematically progressed through Concept Maturity Levels while exploring multiple mission architectures via Exploratory Analytic Cases. The presentation will status across three primary technology development tracks: coronagraph systems, ultra-stable telescope technologies, and high-sensitivity UV/visible instrumentation.    This presentation will provide an overview of the technical and programmatic status on HWO-TMPO's progress toward Mission Concept Review.

Items.Authors: Stuart D. Bale
Items.Title: LuSEE-Night: A low lrequency radio pathfinder for the lunar farside
Items.Abstract: The NASA/DOE LuSEE Night experiment [Bale et al. (2023), arXiv:2301.10345] will be deployed on the lunar farside in late 2026 to make full-Stokes spectral measurements of the radio sky below 50 MHz using a simple crossed-dipole antenna system. LuSEE Night will be a pathfinder for future farside observatories, demonstrating many of the (quite ambitious) technologies required to make synoptic, radio quiet measurements throughout the lunar night. A ’stretch’ goal of LuSEE Night is the first measurement of the 21cm spectral features associated with very high redshift (z~100) universe. The foregrounds to this signal will be dominant by several orders of magnitude but offer their own novel scientific opportunities

Items.Authors: Hanshin Lee, Uma Subash, Menelaos K. Poutous
Items.Title: Reactive ion-plasma etched diffraction gratings for astronomy: production of science-grade 4x4 square inch gratings
Items.Abstract: We have been advancing the Reactive-Ion Plasma Etching (RIPLE) process for large surface-area fabrication of diffraction gratings for Astronomy. Earlier, we demonstrated the RIPLE process to be highly deterministic and presented near theoretical super-broadband diffraction efficiencies from several prototype 1x1 sq. inch RIPLE gratings. Standing upon this success, we forged ahead to scale the process to the primary 4x4 sq. inch target area. This areal scaling has been the core of the NSF-RIPLE program which was recently completed. The program’s main outcomes are the four copies of science-grade RIPLE gratings for the VIRUS2 instrument and demonstrates the mature RIPLE process that can result in deeply etched super-efficient large gratings for astronomical applications. In this paper, we describe the characteristics of these diffraction gratings and discuss some of the key methodologies, models, and measurements used in the scaling effort.

Items.Authors: Bruce C. Bigelow, Chris Madden, Francisco Meza, Eduardo Villar, Miroslav Vulinovic
Items.Title: The GMT site, enclosure, and facilities: 2026 design and construction update
Items.Abstract: The Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT) is one of three extremely large telescopes (ELTs) currently in design or construction. The GMT site is located on the summit of Cerro Las Campanas, a peak within the property of the Las Campanas Observatory (LCO) in Chile. The GMT employs seven 8.4m monolithic mirrors as segments to form a single optical surface with an equivalent diameter of 25.4 meters. Developing a new observatory for cutting-edge science operations and a 50-year lifespan poses a variety of design and construction challenges. This paper reports on progress since June, 2024, and addresses the latest developments for the GMT site master plan, completion of the enclosure design, final CFD modeling of the enclosure design, completion of the conceptual and preliminary design phases (and reviews) for the Summit Support Building, and design of the site infrastructure, including a detailed trade study for a ~5 Mega-Watt photo-voltaic power station and battery storage system.

Items.Authors: Claire L. Poppett, David Schlegel
Items.Title: Spec-S5: a next-generation all-sky spectroscopic facility enabling large-scale surveys for cosmology and astrophysics
Items.Abstract: The Stage-5 Spectroscopic Experiment (Spec-S5) is a next-generation, all-sky spectroscopic facility designed to address fundamental questions in cosmology and astrophysics. Building on the legacy of DESI, Spec-S5 will upgrade two existing 4-m telescopes into 6-m wide-field observatories, each equipped with a highly multiplexed spectrograph capable of measuring 13,000 spectra simultaneously. This overview paper summarizes the science motivation, system architecture, and integration strategy of the project. Spec-S5 will deliver a more than tenfold increase in spectroscopic capability, enabling transformative surveys in the post-Rubin, post-DESI era and advancing our understanding of dark matter, dark energy, and cosmic structure formation.

Items.Authors: David Schiminovich, Nicole D. Melso, Meghna Sitaram, Ignacio Cevallos Aleman, Erika T. Hamden
Items.Title: Narrowband integral field spectroscopy and spectropolarimetry: current capabilities and future prospects with advanced optical designs, metamaterials and detectors
Items.Abstract: We present design concepts and prototype performance of next-generation technologies for narrowband integral field spectrographs (NB-IFS) with moderate to high velocity resolution (R ~10,000–40,000), engineered to push extremely low–surface brightness emission detection to new limits. Building on the recent deployment of CHαS—the Circumgalactic H-alpha Spectrograph on the MDM 2.4m telescope—we are advancing NB-IFS concepts for ground- and space-based platforms that challenge assumptions of conventional design. Several concepts replace core components—including the filter, slicer, collimator, grating, and camera—with optical metasurfaces, effectively reimagining the CHαS IFU as a narrowband, highly dispersive, wavelength-routing metalens array. Some also provide full-Stokes spectropolarimetric separation. We compare these to state-of-the-art systems and outline a path to sensitivity gains using photon-counting detectors and, further ahead, non-local Fourier-filtering metasurfaces.

Items.Authors: Roberto Neri, Karl Friedrich Schuster
Items.Title: NOEMA in the wideband era - dual-band receivers and full-stokes polarimetry
Items.Abstract: NOEMA is the most sensitive millimeter/submillimeter interferometer in the northern hemisphere, offering high sensitivity, high resolution imaging across 70–373 GHz. The new Dual-Band upgrade enables full sensitivity observations of 7.7 GHz IF bandwidth per polarization and sideband simultaneously in both the 3 and 1 mm bands. The two identical advanced wideband correlators PolyFiX 1 and 2 deliver 62 GHz of instantaneous complete high-resolution spectral coverage. This crucially accelerates line surveys, provides high precision continuum measurements for SED determinations, reduces calibration systematics through band-to-band phase referencing, and opens new possibilities for transient astrophysics. A major new capability is full-Stokes polarimetry, with Band 1 foreseen for general users in 2026. NOEMA enables spatially resolved studies of magnetic fields, astrochemistry, star and planet formation, and galaxy evolution.

Items.Authors: Roberta Zanin, Volker Heinz, Bernhard Lopez, David Green, David Green, Paolo G. Calisse, Markus Gaug, Michele Doro, Matthias Füssling, Igor Oya, Andrea Cremonini, Vanessa Montes, Orel Gueta, Mieke Bouwhuis, Maurizio Miccolis, Paolo Petrinca
Items.Title: Operating the CTAO: Challenges of a Distributed VHE gamma-ray observatory
Items.Abstract: The Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO) is a next-generation, open and proposal-driven facility for very-high-energy gamma-ray astronomy, operating as an observatory with four places of operation in Italy, Germany, Spain, and Chile. Approaching the deployment of its first intermediate array configuration, the CTAO will soon exceed the performance of current instruments and begin early science operations while progressing toward its baseline configuration. This paper outlines CTAO end-to-end workflow, from proposal preparation and observation planning to data processing and delivery of science-ready products. It highlights the coordination required across its hemispheric stations to optimize scientific return, enable rapid response to transient events, and support MWL and MM studies. A fully integrated atmospheric characterization program ensures control of systematic uncertainties, while tightly coupled technical and scientific operations maintain long term performance.

Items.Authors: Petr Kubánek
Items.Title: Rubin Observatory’s telescope & site software: developing, commissioning, and operating software for a new survey telescope
Items.Abstract: Vera C. Rubin Observatory is an operational integrated observatory located at Cerro Pachon in Chile. The observatory’s software is divided into two parts. The Data Management part, and the telescope and site part. This part handles commanding all hardware components of the observatory and reading telemetry from all the sensors. The data management handles data observed by LSSTCam and the auxiliary telescope spectrograph. Those parts are linked together - data processing needs data acquired by the observatory, and the observatory needs feedback from the data to improve its optical alignment. This article describes the telescope and site part. It is a story of developing in-house drivers for complete assemblies and integrating delivered components into the software. The story of development in various programming languages and paradigms, of team building, testing, and operating the system together for the benefit of the observatory and its community.

Items.Authors: Matthew R. Bolcar, Feng Zhao, Paul Scowen, Lee Feinberg, Jeffrey S. Smith, Josh Abel
Items.Title: The Habitable Worlds Observatory technology development plan
Items.Abstract: The Habitable Worlds Observatory is NASA’s next large space telescope, selected by the 2020 Decadal Survey in Astronomy and Astrophysics to search for and characterize habitable exoplanets while enabling a broad range of transformative astrophysics. The HWO Technology Maturation Project Office (TMPO) is exploring the HWO science, technology, and mission architectures toward a Mission Concept Review (MCR) at the end of the decade. A primary deliverable of this effort is a technology development plan that identifies critical technologies that enable the mission, defines a process for assessing the readiness of those technologies, and outlines a strategy for developing those technologies to a Technology Readiness Level (TRL) of 5 before the MCR. In this paper we summarize the HWO technology development plan which comprises three “tracks”: Coronagraph System technologies, Ultra-stable Telescope System technologies, and High-sensitivity Ultraviolet and Visible Instrumentation technologies.

Items.Authors: Amirhossein Kermani, Marcello Agostino Scalera, Matteo Genoni, Marco Riva, Alessio Zanutta
Items.Title: Towards AI-assisted AstroMBSE: building a knowledge corpus from SysML models and TLRs
Items.Abstract: In recent years, Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) has been successfully applied to the design of astronomical instruments thanks to the AstroMBSE framework. However, current practice still relies heavily on manual work to manage the system, and many key activities – such as deriving functional architectures and physical breakdowns from top-level requirements (TLRs) – are still performed by hand, which can be time-consuming and error-prone. In this study, we present the first step towards an AI-assisted AstroMBSE co-pilot: the construction of a structured knowledge corpus from existing AstroMBSE projects. The corpus created in this initial phase will be used as a reusable resource for future work and will support later studies on how to use AI to propose operational scenarios and functional architectures, and to check the quality of system models.

Items.Authors: Konstantin Holzner, Christopher Renkl, Manuel Brekenfeld, Dominik Lentrodt, Leonid P. Yatsenko, Sebastian Hepp, Georg Heinze, Tobias Meyer, Andreas Amarotico, Philipp Putzer, Alexander Niggebaum, Bernward Dimke, Martin Enderlein, Bernhard Ernstberger, Armin Zach, Guillaume Bourdarot, Helmut Feuchtgruber, Frank Eisenhauer, Lauren H. Schatz, Steven M. Massey, Robert L. Johnson, Frank Lison
Items.Title: Return flux measurements of a high-power polychromatic laser guide star
Items.Abstract: Laser guide star (LGS) adaptive optics has become widespread in ground-based astronomy. It is also the most promising approach for countering atmospheric distortions in uplink optical satellite communications and laser-based space debris tracking and manoeuvring. The best performance is achieved when the LGS is created in the sodium layer at 90 km altitude. A major shortcoming of the technique is the tip/tilt indeterminacy of the LGS, which requires an additional reference beacon (natural guide star or satellite downlink), limiting sky coverage or the control of uplink beam wander. We report on recent simulations and on-sky experiments exploring the feasibility of a polychromatic LGS, which enables tip/tilt measurement via the differential tilt between two wavelengths emitted by the sodium guide star. For the experiments, we have used two state-of-the-art > 50-W laser systems at 589 and 569 nm, based on TOPTICA’s second-generation guide star laser platform.

Items.Authors: Mark Wallace, Pascal Martinez
Items.Title: Procurement of the dome and the telescope structure of the ELT: update status report
Items.Abstract: The telescope Main Structure and the Dome of the ELT are being procured by ESO as an integrated system together with the auxiliary building and the service plants and are supplied by the ACe Consortium. The contract was signed in May 2016 and the road to completion is long and winding and paved on all sides with pitfalls. The progress is visible and tangible; the primary and secondary structures are complete, and we are nearing completion of the physical installations (e.g. electrical, and fluid distribution), with commissioning just around the corner. However, there are various challenges yet to be overcome. In this paper we will describe the progress and achievements of the project so far as well as give an outline of the obstacles still on the horizon.

Items.Authors: Sonia Ghosh, Léon Koopmans, Christiaan Brinkerink, David Prinsloo
Items.Title: The Dark‑Ages Explorer (DEX): A new frontier in low-frequency radio astronomy from the far side of the Moon
Items.Abstract: Our understanding of the early Universe has grown with facilities such as JWST and ground-based radio arrays, but periods before the first stars remain inaccessible. This era of Dark Ages is dominated by neutral hydrogen, observable only through the redshifted 21-cm line at very low radio frequencies. Such measurements cannot be made from Earth due to severe radio-frequency interference and ionospheric distortions. The Dark-ages EXplorer (DEX) is a proposed concept of a low-frequency radio interferometer on the farside of the Moon, a radio-quiet location ideal for observations in the frequency range of 7–50 MHz. DEX consists of a 32X32 3-m crossed-dipole antennas. Deployment on the lunar surface may shift antenna positions and orientations, introducing phase errors and beam distortions, in addition to effects of mutual coupling at low frequencies. I will present the concept of DEX and forward-modelling results on how lunar topography and such systematics impact 21-cm power-spectrum.

Items.Authors: Stephen P. Todd, Éamonn Harvey, Anna MacIver, William Taylor, Eduard Muslimov, Kjetil Dohlen, Matthias Tecza, Magali Loupias, Paula Bañares
Items.Title: HARMONI at ELT: line spread functions in a diffraction limited spectrometer
Items.Abstract: HARMONI is the first light, adaptive optics assisted, near-IR integral field spectrograph for the ELT. It covers a spectral range from 800nm to 2450nm with resolving powers from 3000 to 7000 and spatial sampling of 25mas and 6mas. It can operate in two adaptive optics modes - SCAO (including a high contrast capability) and MCAO. The project is resuming its final design phase after a rescope design phase in 2025.   Diffraction of the pupil becomes significant in a spectrograph where the slit width is comparable to the diffraction limited PSF. When the spatial coherence due to the narrow slit is considered, the resulting line spread function can be narrower than the geometric width of the input slit, with a non-linear dependence on the size of the pupil aperture after the slit. We outline the impact of these diffraction and spatial filtering effects on the line spread function of HARMONI and identify parameters that should be considered when designing a diffraction limited spectrograph.

Items.Authors: Paolo Petrinca, Andrea Cremonini, Roberta Zanin, Daniela Simone, Marco Rossi
Items.Title: Bridging science, design, and verification: a model-based architecture for the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO) implements a Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) framework to bridge scientific objectives with system design and verification. This paper details a SysML-based process where the system architecture is derived directly from Science Use Cases, establishing a single Source of Truth. Behavioral modeling is shown to not only generate unambiguous requirements but also support a "Design-Driven" Verification and Validation (V&V) strategy. By mapping behavioral paths directly to test scenarios, complete traceability from scientific goals to test procedures is ensured. This approach facilitates early verification planning, reduces integration risks, and optimizes costs by validating operational logic prior to physical implementation.

Items.Authors: Reinhardt von Brandis-Martini, Tinus Stander
Items.Title: Concept designs for concurrent quad-band sideband separating downconverters
Items.Abstract: Simultaneous observation at multiple frequencies improves radio telescope efficiency by  increasing the data collected per unit observation time, and enables frequency-phase-transfer  (FPT) calibration of VLBI observations. The Korean VLBI network (KVN) represents the  state of the art in concurrent multi-band observation, and employs a quasi-optical front-end.  This solution requires significant cabin volume and duplication of receiver components. We  investigate two multi-mixer topologies to extend a standard sideband separating (2SB) mixer  to a quad-band sideband separating (4SB) downconverter. The resulting image rejection ratios  of 15 dB and conversion loss of 15–20 dB indicate a solution that offers a compact and power-  efficient alternative to a quasi-optical system.

Items.Authors: John D. Monnier
Items.Title: Development of quantum technologies for optical/infrared interferometry
Items.Abstract: Quantum technologies may revolutionize optical interferometry through new means to distribute and preserve electric-field amplitude and phase correlations between widely separated telescopes. After reviewing existing techniques, I survey proposed quantum-sensing and quantum-networking applications and highlight recent laboratory demonstrations of key building blocks. By easing field-transport demands for baselines beyond ~1 km, quantum-enhanced interferometry could enable µas-class astrometry and imaging relevant to exoplanets and supermassive black hole environments.    That said, "going quantum" is not a magic shortcut to sensitivity because many of the most compelling science cases remain photon- and turbulence-limited. I therefore emphasize the practical constraints -- loss, bandwidth, coherence time, synchronization, and wavelength limits of quantum interfaces -- that must also be overcome to make these capabilities useful for astronomy, whether deployed on the ground or from space.

Items.Authors: Julienne Boettger, Ronald Holzlöhner, Felipe Pedreros Bustos, Szymon Gladysz, Christian Fruck, Pierre Haguenauer, David Jenkins, Thomas Pfrommer
Items.Title: Error budget for tip/tilt retrieval from laser guide stars using the Propagation-Delay Method
Items.Abstract: The Propagation-Delay Method proposes that atmospheric tip/tilt can be retrieved from a residual laser guide star (LGS) tip/tilt that arises due to the evolving atmospheric turbulence between the laser uplink and LGS downlink. Even partial recovery of tip/tilt from LGS could already increase integration times on natural guide stars, potentially enabling full sky coverage. However, this differential LGS tip/tilt is expected to be 2–3 orders of magnitude smaller than the NGS tip/tilt and thus could be swamped by noise. We analyse noise and error contributions in the detection process, as well as sensitivity limits for the tip/tilt detection with Shack-Hartmann and pyramid wavefront sensors. Finally, we obtain an error budget by comparing the derived noise contributions with the expected signal power spectra under different turbulence and LGS launch conditions, along with the corresponding signal-to-noise ratio as a function of the relevant system parameters.

Items.Authors: Paul A. Scowen, Kevin France, Chris Packham, Richard Cartwright, Janice Lee, Evgenya Shkolnik, Allison Youngblood, Jonathan Papa, Joseph Howard, Breann Sitarski, Jason Tumlinson, Alice Liu, Aki Roberge, Grace Sweetak, Brian Fleming
Items.Title: HWO UV instrument studies: bounding conditions and interfaces
Items.Abstract: NASA’s Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) Technology Maturation Project Office (HTMPO) released a call in 2026 for US-led instrument studies. The instrument concepts should be designed to meet the transformative astrophysics measurement capabilities defined by the Community Science and Instrumentation Team (CSIT) in their analysis of science cases developed by the international astronomical community. The instrument study call defined bounding conditions such as mass, power and volume, as well as a fundamental understanding of the optical, mechanical and thermal interfaces provided by the latest two observatory design concepts. The ultraviolet instrument (UVI) coordination team developed these bounding conditions in 2025 – 2026 with a view to the likely range of capabilities for those instruments. While the NASA-sponsored instrument study call focuses on US-led proposals, NASA fully supports collaborative efforts for instrument studies and designs from international partners.

Items.Authors: Amanda Ibsen
Items.Title: Making sense of metrics: monitoring the performance of the Rubin Observatory control system
Items.Abstract: The health of the Rubin Observatory Control System needs to be continuously monitored in order to ensure its performance. In this work we present how the observatory software team uses metrics such as memory and CPU utilization, inter-component messaging latency, and throttling indicators to rapidly detect and diagnose issues, presenting real-life examples and the practical lessons learned from them.

Items.Authors: Michael S. Schubnell, Timothy Fanning, Andrew Hope, Joseph Silber, Greg Tarlé, Nicholas Wenner
Items.Title: Concept and experimental validation of a hybrid piezoelectric bender fiber positioner
Items.Abstract: We present a novel R-Theta fiber positioner for next-generation spectroscopic instruments, addressing the dense array and fine-pitch needs of future dark energy surveys like Spec-S5. Our hybrid design decouples the two axes: Theta (rotation) uses a compact gearmotor, while radial (R) movement is achieved via a piezoceramic bender. This enables compact packaging, rapid and accurate closed-loop positioning, minimal interference, and cost efficiency. Closed-loop control uses a fiber view camera and centroid algorithm to counter piezo actuator creep and hysteresis. Prototype tests demonstrate micron-level accuracy and reliability at 2-second feedback intervals, showing strong scalability for the fiber densities required by Spec-S5.

Items.Authors: Thomas M. Herbst, Markus Feldt, Pascal Birckigt, Reinhard Geiß, Matthias Goy, Stefan Risse, Silvia Scheithauer, Uwe D. Zeitner
Items.Title: A hybrid grism for efficient space-based slitless spectroscopy
Items.Abstract: We describe our efforts to design and test an entirely new class of optical device for slitless spectroscopy from space. By using nanostructured hybrid gratings, we can devote a fraction (typically 10%) of the telescope pupil to direct imaging, with the remainder allocated to spectroscopy. This permits simultaneous measurement of the “ground-truth” image and the dispersed light, and it allows flexible placement of the image and spectrum on a single detector. We report on our progress using two different approaches: 1. Integration of monolithic prisms onto lithographic gratings using robotic and interferometrically-controlled alignment systems; and 2. Production of nano-gratings and micro-prisms directly on a wafer using lithography only. The eventual goal is to produce at least two prototypes that we can test in the lab and at a ground-based observatory.

Items.Authors: Christiaan D. Brinkerink
Items.Title: Making Moon-based neutral hydrogen cosmology possible: current technology development towards the Dark-ages EXplorer (DEX)
Items.Abstract: The design and development of an instrument that can perform neutral hydrogen cosmology from the lunar far side presents a wide range of technical challenges, which is why current efforts of the Astrophysical Lunar Observatory topical team (ALO TT) focus on the development of technology that will make such a system possible. This includes ultra-low mass antenna systems, novel antenna deployment systems, temperature-tolerant electronics and low-power signal processing. In this contribution, I give an overview of the ongoing technology maturation efforts as well as the next steps in this larger context. These concrete efforts include the development of foil-based antenna systems and novel approaches to low-power radio receiver hardware.
